title: What is an ETF? A complete beginner guide
seoTitle: What Is an ETF? Complete Beginner Guide to Exchange-Traded Funds
seoDescription: Learn how ETFs work, what they hold, how they trade, what fees and tracking error mean, and what risks investors should understand.
excerpt: An ETF is a fund whose shares trade on an exchange, giving investors access to a basket of assets through one security.
author: KitsuWire Editorial
keyTakeaways: An ETF is a fund that trades on an exchange like a stock.
Many ETFs track an index, but others follow sectors, bonds, commodities or active strategies.
Diversification can reduce single-company risk, but an ETF is only as safe as the assets and strategy it contains.
Fees, liquidity, tracking difference, taxes and structure all matter when evaluating an ETF.
body: An exchange-traded fund, or ETF, is an investment fund whose shares can be bought and sold on an exchange during the trading day. Instead of purchasing every asset in a portfolio individually, an investor can gain exposure through one fund share.
ETFs have become popular because they can combine diversification, transparency and relatively simple trading. But the label ETF does not automatically mean low risk or low cost.

sections.heading: How an ETF works
paragraphs: An ETF holds a portfolio according to its stated strategy. A broad equity ETF might own hundreds or thousands of companies, while a sector ETF may hold only businesses from one industry.

Investors trade ETF shares with each other on an exchange. Behind the scenes, authorized participants can create or redeem large blocks of shares, helping keep the market price close to the value of the underlying holdings.

sections.heading: Index ETFs and active ETFs
paragraphs: Many ETFs are passive and aim to track an index. Their goal is not to pick winners but to replicate the performance of a defined benchmark before fees and tracking differences.
Active ETFs give a manager more discretion over which assets to hold. That flexibility may create opportunities, but it also introduces manager risk and can involve higher costs.

sections.heading: Diversification and concentration
paragraphs: A broad ETF can spread exposure across many companies or securities, reducing dependence on the success of one issuer. This is one reason ETFs are often used as building blocks in portfolios.
However, not every ETF is diversified. A thematic or leveraged ETF may be highly concentrated or volatile. Investors need to look through the wrapper and understand what the fund actually owns.

sections.heading: Fees, spreads and tracking difference
paragraphs: The expense ratio is the annual operating cost charged by the fund. Even small differences can matter over long periods, especially when returns are modest.

Trading also involves bid-ask spreads. In addition, an ETF may not perfectly match its benchmark because of fees, taxes, cash holdings, replication methods or market frictions. The gap is often described through tracking difference or tracking error.

sections.heading: Physical vs synthetic replication
paragraphs: A physically replicated ETF buys some or all of the underlying securities. A synthetic ETF can use derivatives, such as swaps, to obtain the desired index exposure.
Synthetic replication can be efficient for difficult markets, but it introduces counterparty and structural considerations that investors should understand.

sections.heading: What risks do ETFs have?
paragraphs: Market risk remains the most important. If the underlying assets decline, the ETF can decline too. Bond ETFs face interest-rate and credit risk; commodity ETFs can behave differently depending on their structure; leveraged products can produce very different long-term results than investors expect.
ETFs are therefore tools, not guarantees. The correct risk assessment starts with the holdings, strategy and structure of the specific fund.

faq.question: Is an ETF the same as an index fund?
faq.answer: Not exactly. Many ETFs are index funds, but an index fund can also be structured as a traditional mutual fund, and some ETFs are actively managed.

faq.question: Can an ETF lose money?
faq.answer: Yes. ETFs reflect the performance and risks of their underlying assets and can fall significantly in value.

faq.question: What is an expense ratio?
faq.answer: It is the annual operating cost of a fund expressed as a percentage of assets.
